placement.title: How to choose a tattoo placement
paragraphs: Start with the shape of the design. Long vertical artwork fits the forearm, spine and ribs, while round compositions sit naturally on the shoulder, chest or thigh. Small symbols need a compact area with enough clear space around them. A reference photographed on the wrong body area can give a misleading idea of scale.

Visibility is the second decision. Hand, finger and neck tattoos are difficult to hide, while chest, thigh and ribs can usually remain private. Clothing, watches, shoes and existing tattoos create practical boundaries. Measure those boundaries before asking an artist to resize a design.

The links above lead to galleries organised by body area. Each image includes an estimated size and style so you can compare like with like. Save several placements, then use the placement picker to narrow the list before your consultation.

Before settling on an area, place a paper outline of the proposed size on your body and photograph it from a normal distance. This exposes scale problems that are difficult to see in a close mirror view and gives the artist a more useful starting point.

subject.title: Turn a subject into a useful tattoo brief
paragraphs: A subject is only the starting point. A flower may be a single front-facing bloom, a botanical stem or part of a larger sleeve. An animal can be a portrait, a moving full-body figure or a simple silhouette. Choose the version before discussing line weight and colour.

Collect references for separate reasons. One image may show the pose, another the amount of detail and a third the placement. Tell the artist what you want to combine instead of asking for a direct copy. This creates a specific brief while leaving room for an original drawing.
Use the subject pages to compare the same motif across several placements and sizes. If the design becomes unclear when reduced, move to a larger body area or simplify the supporting elements.

Meaning can be personal without making the visual brief vague. Write the story in one sentence, then separately list the subject, pose, viewpoint and any symbols that must appear. The artist can respond to both without guessing which details are essential.

When several subjects appeal to you, compare their outer shapes on the intended placement. The option that fits naturally with less cropping or bending usually gives the artist more room to create a clear composition.

style.title: Compare styles at the size you plan to use
paragraphs: Style controls line weight, contrast, colour and the amount of detail a design can carry. Fine line and minimalist work rely on spacing. Traditional designs use bold outlines and compact colour. Realism needs room for value changes, while blackwork depends on the balance between solid areas and open skin.

Do not judge a style only from a close photograph. View examples at the approximate size and distance they will be seen on the body. Check healed work from the artist and look for examples on the same placement you are considering.
Each style page groups references with size and body area labels. Save examples that show the treatment you like, then describe the specific line weight, contrast and palette in your brief.

An artist's portfolio should show consistency in the treatment you want. Look beyond one popular image and compare several finished pieces with similar scale and complexity. A clear body of work is more informative than a broad list of style names.

You can mix influences without asking for several styles at once. Identify the feature you want from each reference, such as bold outlines, restrained shading or a limited palette, and let the artist resolve them into one visual system.

size.title: Measure the design on your body
paragraphs: Centimetres are more useful than labels such as tiny or medium. Print or draw a rectangle at the proposed dimensions and place it on the body. Check it from a normal viewing distance, since a phone screen makes small designs appear much larger than they are.

More detail requires either more space or more simplification. Small designs need a clear outer shape. Medium work can support secondary texture. Large pieces need a full composition with focal points and deliberate open areas.
Use the 3, 5 and 10 cm references in the size guide as a starting point. The final dimensions should follow the body area and the artist's drawing rather than a fixed category name.

Record both height and width in your notes. A ten centimetre line of script and a ten centimetre circular portrait use very different amounts of skin. Dimensions become meaningful only when they are attached to a shape and placement.

Keep a second size option in your shortlist. If the artist recommends more room for lettering, facial features or wing structure, you can compare the larger version without changing the entire concept during the consultation.

for.title: Use audience collections without limiting the design
paragraphs: Audience labels reflect common search language, not rules about who can wear a subject or style. The same flower, animal or geometric design can change completely through scale, placement, colour and line weight. Browse beyond one collection when a reference fits your brief.

For couples, decide whether the tattoos should match, complete one another or share only a visual detail. For individual collections, start with the amount of coverage and visibility you want. Those decisions narrow the options more effectively than a gender label.
Every gallery links back to placement, size, style and subject pages. Save images for their composition and treatment, then combine the useful parts in a description for your artist.

Avoid assuming that the same reference will suit every body. Proportions, existing tattoos and preferred visibility change the final drawing. The collection is a navigation aid, while the artist's stencil is the design made for the individual.

If a category feels too broad, switch to a placement or style page before saving more images. Narrowing by a concrete visual decision produces a more useful shortlist than continuing to browse by audience alone.
